lessons.title: Recognize Common Electrical Products
lessons.why_this_matters: Customers often know what stopped working but not the name of the part.

lesson_content.heading: Know the basics
lesson_content.text: Electrical aisles may include switches, receptacles, cover plates, cords, connectors, breakers, and lighting products. A receptacle is the outlet where a plug connects. A switch controls a circuit or device. These items have different purposes.

lesson_content.heading: Check before recommending
lesson_content.text: Look for the product label and any rating printed on the package. A product that looks similar may have different electrical ratings or installation requirements. Do not assume that matching color or shape means matching function.

lesson_content.heading: Put it into practice
lesson_content.text: Your job is to identify the category and gather information. Never tell a customer to work on energized equipment or bypass a protective device.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer asks for “the thing the lamp plugs into.” Ask whether they mean a wall receptacle, an extension cord, or a power strip before walking them to an aisle.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Ask: “What are you connecting, and can you describe the part you need?” Show labeled product categories without claiming compatibility.
common_mistakes: Handing over a look-alike electrical part without checking its label.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: If the customer describes damaged wiring, sparking, heat, or repeated breaker trips, stop product matching and direct them to qualified help.

optional_practice.question: Which detail best distinguishes a switch from a receptacle?

choices.A: A switch controls; a receptacle accepts a plug
choices.D: Both are types of light bulbs

optional_practice.explanation: A switch controls a circuit or device. A receptacle provides a connection point for a plug.

lessons.title: Read Electrical Labels Without Guessing
lessons.why_this_matters: Similar-looking electrical products may be designed for different conditions.

lesson_content.heading: Know the basics
lesson_content.text: Packages may show voltage, amperage, wattage, location rating, or compatible equipment. Voltage describes electrical potential. Amperage relates to current. Wattage describes power use.

lesson_content.heading: Check before recommending
lesson_content.text: These values are not a license to choose a replacement by appearance. A correct choice also depends on the existing circuit, equipment, installation, and applicable codes.

lesson_content.heading: Put it into practice
lesson_content.text: Point to the label, read the exact wording, and compare it with verified requirements. If the customer cannot confirm those requirements, do not guess.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer wants a replacement breaker based only on its color. Explain that the exact panel and manufacturer compatibility must be confirmed.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Let’s find the model information and check the manufacturer’s listed compatibility.”
common_mistakes: Claiming that any breaker with the same amperage will fit.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate breaker selection, wiring alterations, unclear ratings, and code questions to a qualified electrician or authorized specialist.

lessons.title: Understand Common Lighting Choices
lessons.why_this_matters: A customer may need a specific light output, fit, or use location.

lesson_content.heading: Know the basics
lesson_content.text: Lighting labels often list lumens, watts, color temperature, and base type. Lumens describe light output. Watts describe energy use. Color temperature describes whether the light appears warmer or cooler.

lesson_content.heading: Check before recommending
lesson_content.text: Check the fixture label for bulb type, maximum permitted wattage, and other restrictions. A bulb must physically fit and meet the fixture’s instructions. An enclosed fixture may require a bulb rated for enclosed use.

lesson_content.heading: Put it into practice
lesson_content.text: Dimmable lamps and dimmer controls must be compatible. Outdoor or damp locations require products rated for that environment.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer says their new LED bulb flickers on a dimmer. Ask for the bulb and dimmer models instead of promising that a different wattage will fix it.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Ask: “Is this on a dimmer? Is the fixture enclosed? What base does your current bulb use?”
common_mistakes: Choosing a bulb using only the old bulb’s wattage.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Refer uncertain fixture restrictions or dimmer compatibility to manufacturer documentation or qualified help.

optional_practice.question: Which label most directly describes how much light a bulb produces?
optional_practice.explanation: Lumens measure light output. Watts describe power use.

lessons.title: Match Products to Location and Use
lessons.why_this_matters: An indoor product may be unsafe in a wet or exposed location.

lesson_content.heading: Know the basics
lesson_content.text: Product packages may specify dry, damp, or wet locations. These labels are not interchangeable. Ask where the item will be installed and whether it will face rain, moisture, or other exposure.

lesson_content.heading: Check before recommending
lesson_content.text: Extension cords and power strips have intended uses and ratings. Do not suggest running cords through walls, hiding them under rugs, or using them as permanent wiring.

lesson_content.heading: Put it into practice
lesson_content.text: When a customer requests a solution for a bathroom, garage, porch, or outdoor project, the location matters as much as the product name.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer wants a porch light. Ask whether the fixture will be directly exposed to rain and confirm the manufacturer’s location rating.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Let’s check the package for the installation location it permits.”
common_mistakes: Assuming a product is outdoor-rated because it looks sturdy.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask a qualified electrician about wiring, circuit design, grounding, and code compliance.

lessons.title: Know When Electrical Questions Need an Expert
lessons.why_this_matters: Electrical mistakes can cause fire, shock, or injury.

lesson_content.heading: Know the basics
lesson_content.text: Employees can help locate packaged products and explain terms shown on labels. They should not diagnose live wiring, instruct customers to modify panels, or promise that a repair is code-compliant.

lesson_content.heading: Check before recommending
lesson_content.text: Listen for warning signs: burning smells, warm outlets, sparking, repeated tripping, water near electrical equipment, or exposed conductors. Do not suggest trial-and-error repairs.

lesson_content.heading: Put it into practice
lesson_content.text: Explain the limit without dismissing the customer. Summarize what you know and recommend a licensed electrician or appropriate emergency response for immediate danger.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer reports an outlet that sparked and smells burned. Do not sell a replacement outlet as a complete solution.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “That could be hazardous. Please stop using it and contact a qualified electrician. If there is immediate danger, follow emergency guidance.”
common_mistakes: Treating a potentially dangerous symptom as a simple parts sale.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate hazards immediately according to store policy; use emergency services for an active emergency.
